operationalization: This is a definitional ontology dividing anatomical structures into tissues (homoiomerous parts) and organs (anhomoiomerous parts); no empirical test distinguishes it from alternative mereological definitions.
obstacles: The distinction between uniform and composite parts is conceptual and depends on the spatial scale of subdivision chosen.
rationale: Aristotle's division of body parts into uniform (tissues like flesh and bone) and composite (organs like the hand or face) establishes a foundational anatomical vocabulary rather than an empirical hypothesis. Because any tissue becomes heterogeneous at cellular or molecular scales, the classification is a conceptual convention rather than a falsifiable empirical generalization.

operationalization: As stated by Aristotle, correspondence by analogy is a taxonomic and functional framing across distinct higher genera rather than a phylogenetic or developmental hypothesis with a falsifiable criterion.
obstacles: Aristotle's concept of analogy is a comparative classification rule rather than a testable phylogenetic or developmental claim.
rationale: While modern comparative anatomy tests homology versus convergent analogy using developmental genetics and phylogeny, Aristotle's statement defines how parts across his major animal genera correspond functionally and structurally. As a conceptual principle of comparative morphology, it has no direct empirical decision criterion that would confirm or refute it without importing modern evolutionary definitions.

operationalization: Query dipteran life-history records to check whether Diptera exist with aquatic larvae that metamorphose into terrestrial adults, and specifically whether candidate taxa for Aristotle's 'oistros' (Tabanidae vs. Oestridae or Chironomidae) have aquatic larval stages.

candidate_datasets.name: freshwateranimaldiversityassessment / Freshwater Ecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Larval habitat and life-cycle traits of European aquatic Diptera

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic backbone and life-stage occurrence records for Tabanidae and Chironomidae

obstacles: The Greek term 'oistros' (gadfly) cannot be mapped with certainty to a single modern dipteran family, and candidate families differ in larval habitat.
rationale: The general proposition that some insects have aquatic larvae and aerial adults is trivially confirmed by entomological trait databases. However, resolving the specific claim about the gadfly ('oistros') depends on whether it maps to horseflies (Tabanidae, many of which have aquatic or semi-aquatic larvae) or botflies (Oestridae, which are internal parasites), making the specific claim only partially resolvable due to philological ambiguity.

operationalization: Identify all raptor species (Accipitriformes, Falconiformes, Strigiformes, Cathartiformes) and query avian behavioural and observation databases for communal foraging, roosting, or colonial breeding (flocking behaviour); any raptor exhibiting regular flocking refutes the universal claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological and ecological classifications of raptors worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: eBird Basic Dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Group size counts from field checklists for raptors such as Falco naumanni, Falco vespertinus, and Gyps fulvus

obstacles: Gregariousness must be operationalized across foraging, migration, and colonial nesting contexts.
rationale: Birds with crooked talons map cleanly to modern diurnal and nocturnal raptors. Public avian trait compilations and millions of eBird checklist group-size counts directly test and refute the universal claim, as several Mediterranean raptors (such as the lesser kestrel Falco naumanni, red-footed falcon Falco vespertinus, and griffon vulture Gyps fulvus) are highly gregarious.

operationalization: For each domesticated mammal species named by Aristotle (horse, cattle, pig, sheep, goat, dog) and across all recognized domestic animals, check conservation and taxonomic databases for extant or historically attested wild conspecifics or wild progenitor species.

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic mapping of domestic mammals to their wild progenitors and extant wild statuses

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Extant vs. extinct-in-the-wild status of wild progenitors (e.g., Bos primigenius, Equus ferus, Sus scrofa, Capra aegagrus, Ovis gmelini, Canis lupus)

obstacles: Depends on whether feral populations or wild progenitor species count as the 'same kind', and whether historical status in antiquity or present-day extant status is evaluated.
rationale: Mammalian taxonomy and conservation databases comprehensively document both extant wild progenitors (such as wolf, wild boar, bezoar ibex, and mouflon) and extinct-in-the-wild progenitors (such as the aurochs, which was extant in Aristotle's time) for every named species. The claim can be cleanly evaluated using standard zoological reference databases.

operationalization: Query cross-species anatomical ontologies for the presence/absence of a urinary bladder and an intestine across major animal clades; confirm whether P(intestine | urinary bladder) = 1 and P(urinary bladder | intestine) < 1.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon multi-species anatomy ontology
candidate_datasets.role: Taxon constraints and anatomical presence/absence annotations for urinary bladder (UBERON:0001255) and intestine (UBERON:0000160)

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative vertebrate character matrices for urogenital and digestive tract organs

obstacles: Requires restricting 'bladder' to the vertebrate urinary bladder rather than analogous excretory vesicles in some flatworms or rotifers.
rationale: Presence and absence of the urinary bladder and intestine across vertebrate and invertebrate clades are thoroughly encoded in comparative anatomy ontologies and zoological datasets. Because all vertebrates with a urinary bladder possess a digestive tract with an intestine, while birds, most reptiles, and many fishes possess an intestine without a urinary bladder, existing structured data resolve the claim directly.

operationalization: Assess across basal metazoan phyla (Porifera, Placozoa, Cnidaria, Ctenophora) and Bilateria whether mechanosensation (touch) is universally present while vision, hearing, olfaction, and gustation are absent in some clades.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic distribution of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo, TRP) and chemoreceptor/photoreceptor families across Metazoa

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon multi-species anatomy ontology
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic distribution of specialized sensory organs across animal phyla

obstacles: Distinguishing 'touch' (mechanosensation) from 'taste' (chemosensation) at the cellular level in sponges and placozoans is conceptually ambiguous because both exist without nervous systems.
rationale: Comparative physiology and genomic databases clearly show that specialized organs for vision and hearing are absent in many animals, whereas mechanical responsiveness and mechanosensitive channels (such as Piezo) exist across all metazoans, including sponges and placozoans. However, because chemosensitivity is equally ubiquitous across basal metazoans, resolving whether touch is the 'only' universal sense depends on how touch versus taste is operationalized in aneural animals.

operationalization: Map 'animals with blood' to Vertebrata and 'bloodless animals' to Invertebrata; check limb-count distributions across all extant animal phyla to test whether all species with >4 walking appendages are invertebrates and all vertebrates have 0, 2, or 4 limbs.

candidate_datasets.name: Encyclopedia of Life (EOL) TraitBank
candidate_datasets.role: Body plan and appendage count records across vertebrate and invertebrate clades

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Paired appendage counts across gnathostome and tetrapod vertebrates

obstacles: Requires equating Aristotle's 'blooded' (enhaima) with red-blooded vertebrates rather than invertebrates that possess hemoglobin.
rationale: Under the standard taxonomic mapping of Aristotle's 'blooded' animals to vertebrates and 'bloodless' animals to invertebrates, limb number is a fundamental body-plan trait recorded across all zoological databases. Every vertebrate has at most four locomotor limbs (0, 2, or 4), and every animal with more than four legs (insects, arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods, cephalopods) is an invertebrate.

operationalization: Compare embryonic cleavage and yolk utilization in macrolecithal vertebrate eggs (meroblastic cleavage where the blastodisc forms the embryo and yolk provides nutrition) with insect larva ('grub') metamorphosis where the entire larval body reorganizes into the pupa/imago.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon multi-species anatomy ontology
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental ontology terms and taxon constraints for meroblastic cleavage, embryonic disc, yolk sac, and holometabolous larva

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA (Gallus Expression in Situ Hybridization Analysis)
candidate_datasets.role: Avian embryonic staging and blastoderm vs. yolk development data

obstacles: Aristotle contrasts true eggs with insect 'grubs' (larvae), which are actually post-hatching stages of microlecithal/centrolecithal insect eggs.
rationale: In macrolecithal eggs of birds, reptiles, and selachians (which Aristotle classifies as true eggs), embryological data confirm that the embryo forms from the blastodisc while the yolk mass serves as nutrient reserve. Similarly, developmental data confirm that an insect larva ('grub') transforms as a whole organism into the pupa and adult rather than budding from a fraction of its mass.

operationalization: Query reproductive mode classifications in FishBase for Selachii (sharks) and in mammalian trait databases for Eutheria to verify whether sharks exhibit ovoviviparity (aplacental/placental viviparity via intrauterine egg hatching) while mammals develop a live fetus directly in utero.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive guild and mode (ovoviviparity, viviparity, oviparity) for shark species

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Viviparous reproductive traits for horses, humans, and other mammals

rationale: Reproductive modes of cartilaginous fishes and mammals are standard categorical variables in FishBase and mammalian trait databases. Existing data directly confirm that most viviparous sharks develop from encapsulated eggs that hatch inside the uterus before live birth, in contrast to placental mammals.

operationalization: Compare maximum body size distributions of invertebrate taxa across marine, freshwater, and terrestrial realms and across latitudinal/thermal zones using global marine and terrestrial trait databases.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)
candidate_datasets.role: Body size attributes and habitat classification (marine, brackish, freshwater, terrestrial) for invertebrate species

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS)
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced occurrence and sea surface temperature data to map invertebrate size across thermal regimes

obstacles: Deep-sea/polar gigantism in some marine clades (e.g., colossal squid, giant isopods) complicates the latitudinal 'milder climate' comparison unless restricted to shallow coastal and terrestrial fauna.
rationale: Global invertebrate trait and occurrence databases allow direct statistical comparison of maximum body lengths across marine, freshwater, and terrestrial habitats, as well as across climatic zones. Marine invertebrates (cephalopods, decapod crustaceans, bivalves) clearly reach much larger maximum sizes than terrestrial or freshwater invertebrates, and latitudinal body-size gradients can be tested directly.

operationalization: Query comprehensive mammalian trait datasets for all hair-coated species (class Mammalia) and check whether any species are oviparous rather than viviparous.

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE: a coalesced mammal database of intrinsic and extrinsic traits
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive mode (viviparity vs. oviparity) across all extant mammal species

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Complete taxonomic list of Mammalia including Monotremata, Marsupialia, and Placentalia

rationale: Hair-coated animals map exactly to Mammalia. Comprehensive mammal trait databases immediately test this universal claim: it holds for all placental and marsupial mammals (including all Old World mammals known to Aristotle), but is refuted globally by the five extant species of hair-coated, egg-laying monotremes (platypus and echidnas, including spiny echidnas).

operationalization: Compare cranial suture topology (presence of coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid sutures vs. a single circular suture) between male and female human crania in osteological and medical imaging datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: Howells Craniometric Data Set
candidate_datasets.role: Osteological reference populations (preferring open clinical/cranial CT repositories below)

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: Public structural cranial CT and MRI scans of male and female human subjects

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA)
candidate_datasets.role: High-resolution head CT scans with sex metadata showing cranial sutures

rationale: Cranial suture anatomy in male and female humans is directly observable in thousands of publicly available head CT scans and documented osteological collections. Both males and females possess the same sagittal, coronal, and lambdoid suture pattern, decisively refuting the claim.
